subcomponents.title: Uses stable identities and appropriate grouped-scene architecture

criteria.rationale: All nine steps come from one TABLE.map in steps.ts. Each gets groupKey 'scene' and the same Scene component, and only payload.stage varies. Stage keys its motion.div with sceneKey(step), which returns `group:${groupKey}:${sceneId(Scene)}`, so the same key is produced for all nine steps and the scene instance persists with only its payload changing. Entity identity is separate. The presentation-owned ENTITIES/EntityId list drives Scene: it filters ENTITIES by FIRST_STEP and keys each Appear by the id. The ids 'reveal-label' and the `morph-${link}` chips are literal ids outside ENTITIES but are equally stable. criteria.rationale: Unmet clause: when an entity with the same identity is in two consecutive ungrouped steps, it should animate from its old state to its new state in place. With the kit's entity primitives, it instead vanishes and reappears. Mechanism: - Steps with no groupKey get their own key (sceneKey.ts:16-20, step:${step.id}). - Stage wraps each keyed scene in one AnimatePresence (sync mode) inside a LayoutGroup. The outgoing scene fades out over STEP_FADE_T = 0.4s (Stage.tsx:29-42; constants.ts:9). - Stage's initial={false} only covers children present on the first render. An incoming keyed scene still runs its opacity 0 to 1 fade. The auditor's open question is answered by SceneLayer.tsx:13-21. SceneLayer renders a plain <AnimatePresence>{children}</AnimatePresence> with no initial={false}. A newly mounted scene creates a new SceneLayer, so each Appear child in it plays its initial state. - Appear's initial state is initial={{ opacity: 0 }}, with a fade-in delayed by ENTER_DELAY (Appear.tsx:17-28). - ENTER_DELAY = LAYOUT_T = 0.6s (constants.ts:4-9). That is longer than the 0.4s scene fade. - Appear wraps the layout-animated NodeBase (layout, layoutId={id}, Node.tsx:26-38). So the incoming copy's layout morph runs while an opacity-0 ancestor hides it. - The outgoing copy fades out within 0.4s. The incoming copy only starts fading in at 0.6s, after its 0.6s layout morph has ended. - This is exactly the 'fixed initial opacity of 0 with an entrance delay as long as the step transition' failure the guidance names. - The delivered sample renders every entity through this path (<SceneLayer> containing <Appear key={id}>, Scene.tsx:148-156). Why Judge A's pass does not decide the criterion: A says NodeBase and Arrow do not impose initial opacity zero. That is true of NodeBase on its own (Node.tsx:26-38). But it ignores the kit's Appear wrapper and SceneLayer, the kit's presence boundary for entities, which the sample uses for every entity. Those hide the incoming copy past the cross-fade. A sync-mode, out-of-flow Stage alone does not establish a pass. Judges B and C reach the same conclusion this source shows.

criteria.rationale: Newcomer entry path: Appear starts at opacity 0 and fades in over ENTER_T = 0.4s, after a delay that defaults to ENTER_DELAY = LAYOUT_T = 0.6s. The delay is set on Appear's own animate transition, so it applies only to the newcomer's opacity entry. Continuing-entity path: NodeBase and Arrow use `layout` and `layoutId` and set no transition prop. A persisting entity keeps its keyed Appear mounted (Scene.tsx lines 152-154), so it does not replay the delayed fade and only its layout projection runs. The sample sets no MotionConfig or layout transition anywhere; a grep for MotionConfig, transition= and LAYOUT_T finds only Stage's scene-opacity transition and test and constant uses. The continuing layout morph therefore runs on Motion's default layout transition (about 0.45s), which ends before the 0.6s newcomer delay elapses. That default comes from the Motion library, not this repo; the source establishes only that nothing overrides it. Every entity the sample introduces is rendered inside `<Appear key={id}>`. Nested identities share their parent's delayed Appear and stay invisible until it enters: the morph chips inside the link entries, reveal-label inside the reveal-frame entry, and pass-check inside a span. motion-props.test.tsx asserts that Appear's delay is at least LAYOUT_T and equals ENTER_DELAY. Judges B and C reach this verdict from the same material. Judge A's fail reason is that the continuing layout duration is not set by LAYOUT_T and not verified by a test. That does not decide the criterion. The guidance credits a fixed configured delay at least as long as the continuing layout transition, and requires no shared settlement contract or focused test. The layout path the continuing entities actually use is the unoverridden default, which is shorter than the delay.

subcomponents.title: Fixed-canvas uniform viewport fitting

subcomponents.title: Verification tooling robustness

criteria.rationale: I rule with judges A and B. In all four script copies (repository and bootstrap verify and inspect), startPreview spawns `process.execPath` running node_modules/vite/bin/vite.js directly, with `detached: true` (preview.mjs:95-112). No npm or npx wrapper sits in between, so the child pid is the server process and leads its own process group. Its stop function is `installCleanup(() => killGroup(child.pid), ...)` (line 104). killGroup sends SIGTERM to `-pid`, the whole group, then polls `isPidAlive` every 50 ms during the grace period (lines 29-41). isPidAlive (lines 19-26) is `process.kill(pid, 0)`, which returns false once the process no longer exists. If readiness fails, startPreview awaits stop() before rethrowing (lines 105-110). verify() runs chromium.launch(), newPage and renderSteps inside `try`, and the `finally` awaits `browser?.close()` and then `preview.stop()` (verify.mjs:180-189, same in the bootstrap copy). So success, a failing check, a browser launch failure and any later error all pass through that cleanup. In inspect(), `outputDir(...)` (line 196) sits between startPreview and `try`, which the auditor raised. It cannot throw on any path the script takes. The script's only entry point, main(), calls inspect with `parseArgs(...)` (lines 235-243). parseArgs rejects any slug that fails `SLUG = /^[a-z0-9]+(-[a-z0-9]+)*$/` before inspect runs (line 32). For a slug that passes, `path.join(artifacts, slug)` is always a direct child of OUT_DIR, so none of outputDir's throw conditions can hold (lines 42-50). Everything after it is inside try/finally with `await preview.stop()` (lines 198-232). The bootstrap copies are identical (parity.test.ts asserts byte equality). Signals and a bare process exit are also covered by installCleanup. Judge C's reason is that after the grace period killGroup sends SIGKILL without polling again. That branch runs only when a server ignores SIGTERM for 1.5 s, and nothing cited shows vite preview doing so. SIGKILL to the group cannot be ignored, and the focused test 'escalates to SIGKILL when SIGTERM is ignored' confirms the group dies. The E2E tests confirm that after both passing and failing verify runs the preview pid is no longer running and its port is closed. A hypothetical that the source does not produce does not make the requirement unmet.

The mismatch with the ledger is minor: the ledger's optional question about whether 7.5 px is readable enough sits beside the handoff's 'no new ambiguity', and the label size is described as 'approximately 8–9 px' where the ledger gives a 7.5 px minimum. Neither shows a demonstrably false or concealed claim.
evidence: Log lists NOT EXERCISED and PARTIALLY EXERCISED items and a 'Deliberately not exercised' section for both rounds.
Log states the synthetic touch events and that physical touch input was not exercised.
Handoff discloses the first-pass skill-interaction limitations, the CI and validation status, the reviewed advisory warnings, and that no automated suites or lint were run.
Findings history records F-001 as resolved and the six advisories as reviewed, not defects.
judging basis: consensus-pass

subcomponents.title: Observable assumption handling

criteria.rationale: The ledger surfaces the consequential ambiguities and records the options considered. These include the target-confirmation condition (a/b/c), the SKILL.md inspection-versus-grep method, the sample's grouping, and the narrow-viewport readability limit with its remaining levers. The exploration log reproduced the one deviation it observed, F-001 (about 4 px diagram text at 390 px). It recorded it as a finding, which the findings history shows resolved in round 1. The six desktop overlap advisories were surfaced and reviewed rather than silently dropped. The log also discloses what was not exercised. I found no recorded deviation from the approved requirements that goes unsurfaced. The attribution URL (and-scene/and-scene) differs from the PR repo org, but the record does not establish that it is the wrong target.
evidence: Ledger entry on target confirmation lists options (a)/(b)/(c) with a ruling and rationale.
Ledger F-001 entry states the 7 px floor is 'my own bar' and lists the remaining levers (per-viewport canvas, pan/zoom, larger canvas).
Exploration log records F-001 as reproduced at about 4 px, then resolved in round 1.
Findings history records the six desktop advisories as reviewed, with their measured 1–2 px range intersections.
judging basis: consensus-pass

criteria.rationale: The ledger separates what the approved definition and repository fix from the candidate's own rulings. It cites CLAUDE.md byte-alignment, design Routing, and the 'spec lists the helper's warnings exhaustively' constraint. It labels the 7 px floor as 'my own bar'. The record does not classify any reproduced violation as acceptable. F-001 was reproduced and treated as a defect, then fixed and retested. The desktop advisories were reviewed against screenshots and range measurements, and the log does not misstate them.
evidence: Ledger: 'The 7 px floor is my own bar, chosen as the largest that fits the nine-beat composition; the definition names none.'
Ledger: 'The tester's report is a defect, not a design limit.'
Ledger parity entry cites CLAUDE.md 'byte-aligned' and the spec.
judging basis: consensus-pass

criteria.rationale: The decisions stay within the approved definition. Rulings such as target confirmation reading (b) and unknown route showing Landing are marked as adding no new gate. The one decision that would change approved behavior, a per-viewport canvas, pan/zoom, or a larger canvas, was not taken and was left as an optional escalation to the user. The ledger also declined to add a helper warning that would change the spec's exhaustive warning list. The escalation is proportionate: no decision was taken without authority.
evidence: Ledger: 'Each [lever] alters the fixed-canvas contract, so none was applied. Tell me which, if any, you want.'
Ledger: the helper gets no new 'tiny rendered text' warning because the spec lists its warnings exhaustively.
Ledger: 'Pending from user: None. The ruling stays inside the approved definition and adds no approval gate.'
judging basis: consensus-pass

criteria.rationale: The ledger carries an open optional decision. 'Readability of diagram text at the narrow viewport (acceptance F-001)' leaves 7.5 px as the result and asks the user whether to pursue a per-viewport or portrait canvas, pan/zoom, or a larger canvas. The handoff does not name that decision, its consequence, or the options. It says only 'No new ambiguity was identified in this retest' and 'No new defect or product ambiguity remains', and then points to acceptance-assumptions.md without naming any decision. It also says F-001 shows 'legible' labels without the ledger's caveat that the text is only about 7.5 px, a floor the candidate chose itself. It omits the ledger's other rulings (for example target-confirmation (b)) by name. The handoff does disclose the unexercised skill-dialogue scenarios, but the open narrow-viewport decision is not preserved.
evidence: Handoff 'Assumptions' section: 'Ledger: acceptance-assumptions.md. No new ambiguity was identified in this retest.' No decision is named.
Ledger F-001 entry: 'Pending from user: Optional. If 7.5 px on a phone is not readable enough, the remaining levers change approved behavior…'
Handoff decision brief: 'No new defect or product ambiguity remains.'
judging basis: consensus-fail

result.rationale: Unmet clause: when an entity with the same identity is in two consecutive ungrouped steps, it should animate from its old state to its new state in place. With the kit's entity primitives, it instead vanishes and reappears. Mechanism: - Steps with no groupKey get their own key (sceneKey.ts:16-20, step:${step.id}). - Stage wraps each keyed scene in one AnimatePresence (sync mode) inside a LayoutGroup. The outgoing scene fades out over STEP_FADE_T = 0.4s (Stage.tsx:29-42; constants.ts:9). - Stage's initial={false} only covers children present on the first render. An incoming keyed scene still runs its opacity 0 to 1 fade. The auditor's open question is answered by SceneLayer.tsx:13-21. SceneLayer renders a plain <AnimatePresence>{children}</AnimatePresence> with no initial={false}. A newly mounted scene creates a new SceneLayer, so each Appear child in it plays its initial state. - Appear's initial state is initial={{ opacity: 0 }}, with a fade-in delayed by ENTER_DELAY (Appear.tsx:17-28). - ENTER_DELAY = LAYOUT_T = 0.6s (constants.ts:4-9). That is longer than the 0.4s scene fade. - Appear wraps the layout-animated NodeBase (layout, layoutId={id}, Node.tsx:26-38). So the incoming copy's layout morph runs while an opacity-0 ancestor hides it. - The outgoing copy fades out within 0.4s. The incoming copy only starts fading in at 0.6s, after its 0.6s layout morph has ended. - This is exactly the 'fixed initial opacity of 0 with an entrance delay as long as the step transition' failure the guidance names. - The delivered sample renders every entity through this path (<SceneLayer> containing <Appear key={id}>, Scene.tsx:148-156). Why Judge A's pass does not decide the criterion: A says NodeBase and Arrow do not impose initial opacity zero. That is true of NodeBase on its own (Node.tsx:26-38). But it ignores the kit's Appear wrapper and SceneLayer, the kit's presence boundary for entities, which the sample uses for every entity. Those hide the incoming copy past the cross-fade. A sync-mode, out-of-flow Stage alone does not establish a pass. Judges B and C reach the same conclusion this source shows.

checks.rationale: I'm rejecting the dissent. Its facts are accurate, but they don't decide the requirement. The dissent says the continuing entities' layout duration isn't set by LAYOUT_T and isn't checked by a test. The guidance credits a fixed configured delay that is at least as long as the layout transition the continuing entities actually run. It does not require a shared settlement contract, an observed completion signal, or a focused test. Newcomer entry path: in `src/presentation-kit/nodes/Appear.tsx`, `Appear` starts at opacity 0. It fades in over ENTER_T = 0.4s after a delay of ENTER_DELAY = LAYOUT_T = 0.6s, both from `src/presentation-kit/constants.ts`. That delay sits only inside Appear's own `animate.transition`, so it affects only the newcomer's opacity entry. Continuing-entity path: `NodeBase` in `src/presentation-kit/nodes/Node.tsx` and `Arrow` in `src/presentation-kit/nodes/Arrow.tsx` set `layout` and `layoutId` and no transition. The sample's `Scene.tsx` passes no transition, and `Stage.tsx` has no MotionConfig; its only transition is the scene-level opacity cross-fade. So the layout morph runs on Motion's default layout transition, which lasts about 0.45s and ends before the 0.6s delay. That default comes from the Motion library, not this repo; the source only shows that nothing overrides it. A persisting entity keeps its keyed `<Appear key={id}>` mounted, so it does not replay the delayed fade. Every entity the sample introduces renders inside a delayed Appear, including the morph chips, `reveal-label` (inside `reveal-frame`) and `pass-check` (inside a span). None appears without entry motion. The dissent does not answer the majority's reason: the delay outlasts the unoverridden layout transition, and it applies to the newcomer's entry only.

scene-kit.rationale: Newcomer entry path: Appear starts at opacity 0 and fades in over ENTER_T = 0.4s, after a delay that defaults to ENTER_DELAY = LAYOUT_T = 0.6s. The delay is set on Appear's own animate transition, so it applies only to the newcomer's opacity entry. Continuing-entity path: NodeBase and Arrow use `layout` and `layoutId` and set no transition prop. A persisting entity keeps its keyed Appear mounted (Scene.tsx lines 152-154), so it does not replay the delayed fade and only its layout projection runs. The sample sets no MotionConfig or layout transition anywhere; a grep for MotionConfig, transition= and LAYOUT_T finds only Stage's scene-opacity transition and test and constant uses. The continuing layout morph therefore runs on Motion's default layout transition (about 0.45s), which ends before the 0.6s newcomer delay elapses. That default comes from the Motion library, not this repo; the source establishes only that nothing overrides it. Every entity the sample introduces is rendered inside `<Appear key={id}>`. Nested identities share their parent's delayed Appear and stay invisible until it enters: the morph chips inside the link entries, reveal-label inside the reveal-frame entry, and pass-check inside a span. motion-props.test.tsx asserts that Appear's delay is at least LAYOUT_T and equals ENTER_DELAY. Judges B and C reach this verdict from the same material. Judge A's fail reason is that the continuing layout duration is not set by LAYOUT_T and not verified by a test. That does not decide the criterion. The guidance credits a fixed configured delay at least as long as the continuing layout transition, and requires no shared settlement contract or focused test. The layout path the continuing entities actually use is the unoverridden default, which is shorter than the delay.

votes.rationale: Readiness comes from HTTP polling (`fetch(url)` with res.ok) of the chosen port. The only ownership check is `child.exitCode !== null`, sampled before each request. The spawn uses stdio 'ignore', so the child's own announcement is never read. Neither accepted mechanism is present: readiness is not taken from the child's announcement, and polling is not raced against the child's exit. A stale server on the port would answer the fetch before the child's exit is observed. This is possible with VERIFY_PORT, which verify.mjs passes in as a fixed port. It is also possible in the gap after findFreePort closes its probe socket. --strictPort alone is insufficient.

votes.rationale: Readiness comes from HTTP polling of the port. The child is spawned with stdio 'ignore', so it announces nothing. waitReady only samples child.exitCode at the top of each loop iteration, before each fetch. checks.rationale: The dissent is right about the code: in killGroup, the SIGKILL branch returns without polling again. But that branch runs only when the preview server ignores SIGTERM for the 1.5 s grace period. That scenario is not named in the review guidance, and the source does not show Vite preview producing it. SIGKILL cannot be ignored, and the focused test 'escalates to SIGKILL when SIGTERM is ignored' confirms the group dies. On every exit path the guidance names (success, a failing check, a browser launch failure, an error after the preview started), all four copies stop the preview. The server is spawned directly as a detached `node vite.js preview` process, with no npm or npx wrapper. verify() and inspect() await preview.stop() in a finally block that also covers chromium.launch() and all later work. startPreview awaits stop() before rethrowing if readiness fails. Sending SIGTERM to the group, then polling until the pid is gone, satisfies the terminate-and-await requirement on those paths. The dissent's fact is accurate, but the requirement does not depend on it, and it does not answer the majority's reasons.

result.rationale: I rule with judges A and B. In all four script copies (repository and bootstrap verify and inspect), startPreview spawns `process.execPath` running node_modules/vite/bin/vite.js directly, with `detached: true` (preview.mjs:95-112). No npm or npx wrapper sits in between, so the child pid is the server process and leads its own process group. Its stop function is `installCleanup(() => killGroup(child.pid), ...)` (line 104). killGroup sends SIGTERM to `-pid`, the whole group, then polls `isPidAlive` every 50 ms during the grace period (lines 29-41). isPidAlive (lines 19-26) is `process.kill(pid, 0)`, which returns false once the process no longer exists. If readiness fails, startPreview awaits stop() before rethrowing (lines 105-110). verify() runs chromium.launch(), newPage and renderSteps inside `try`, and the `finally` awaits `browser?.close()` and then `preview.stop()` (verify.mjs:180-189, same in the bootstrap copy). So success, a failing check, a browser launch failure and any later error all pass through that cleanup. In inspect(), `outputDir(...)` (line 196) sits between startPreview and `try`, which the auditor raised. It cannot throw on any path the script takes. The script's only entry point, main(), calls inspect with `parseArgs(...)` (lines 235-243). parseArgs rejects any slug that fails `SLUG = /^[a-z0-9]+(-[a-z0-9]+)*$/` before inspect runs (line 32). For a slug that passes, `path.join(artifacts, slug)` is always a direct child of OUT_DIR, so none of outputDir's throw conditions can hold (lines 42-50). Everything after it is inside try/finally with `await preview.stop()` (lines 198-232). The bootstrap copies are identical (parity.test.ts asserts byte equality). Signals and a bare process exit are also covered by installCleanup. Judge C's reason is that after the grace period killGroup sends SIGKILL without polling again. That branch runs only when a server ignores SIGTERM for 1.5 s, and nothing cited shows vite preview doing so. SIGKILL to the group cannot be ignored, and the focused test 'escalates to SIGKILL when SIGTERM is ignored' confirms the group dies. The E2E tests confirm that after both passing and failing verify runs the preview pid is no longer running and its port is closed. A hypothetical that the source does not produce does not make the requirement unmet.

votes.rationale: Readiness is a polling `waitReady` with a deadline (`timeoutMs` defaults to 20000) that throws on timeout. Verify and inspect both run `npm run build` synchronously (`spawnSync`) before calling `startPreview`. Readiness does not parse printed output: the server's stdio is ignored and the script fetches the URL. The ANSI and chunk-splitting clause therefore does not apply.
evidence: `waitReady` in scripts/lib/preview.mjs loops `while (Date.now() < deadline)` and then throws 'preview did not become ready'.
`verify()` calls `runBuild(root)` (spawnSync) before `startPreview`.
`inspect()` runs `spawnSync('npm', ['run','build'])` when `args.build` is true, before `startPreview`.
`startPreview` spawns with `stdio: 'ignore'` and polls with `fetch`, so no printed ready URL is parsed.
The bootstrap template copies are identical.

checks.rationale: The cited material does not support the dissent. The criterion covers the delivered automated tests that drive a browser. Those tests are E2E-001, E2E-002, INT-001 and INT-002. Each one runs `npm run verify` or `npm run inspect` through a synchronous spawnSync helper (tests/e2e/helpers.ts `verify`, tests/integration/run.ts `run`). That call returns only after the subprocess has exited. The tests then assert on its exit status, its output, the report and PNG files it wrote, and the pid and port state. None of these tests calls setTimeout, waitForTimeout or any other sleep. None of them reads an element count as if it had waited. The dissent's point is that the verify and inspect scripts call page.waitForTimeout. Those scripts are verification tooling, not the tests this criterion judges. Even so, the scripts do not use a sleep in place of a state wait. Each ArrowRight is followed by page.waitForFunction, which polls until data-step-index equals the target index. Before any step is read, the scripts wait for the [data-step-count] hook with waitForSelector. The inspect script also polls document.getAnimations() and refuses to capture while an animation is still running. The fixed settle delays come on top of these state waits, and the guidance lists longer fixed settle delays as validator noise. The only fixed `setTimeout(r, 200)` waits in any test are in tests/unit/preview-cleanup.test.ts. That test spawns `sh` processes and drives no browser. So the dissent's fact does not show any browser test sleeping in place of waiting for state.

votes.rationale: No test hardcodes a port. The tests run verify and inspect without setting `VERIFY_PORT`, so `startPreview` allocates a free port via `findFreePort()` (listen on port 0). Every process the tests start is terminated. The e2e tests assert `pidState(preview.pid)` is not running and `portListening(preview.port)` is false after each run, for the success case and for every fault case. The preview-cleanup tests kill the process groups they spawn.

e2e-001 asserts `pidState(preview.pid)` is not 'running' and `await portListening(preview.port)` is false.
e2e-002 repeats those assertions for every fault with `previewStarted: true`.
preview-cleanup.test.ts spawns detached `sh` groups and kills them with `killGroup`/`killGroupSync`, asserting they are gone.
The grep over tests/ found no hardcoded ports.

scene-kit.rationale: computeFit yields one scale, the minimum of availW/DESIGN_W and availH/DESIGN_H, floored at MIN_SCALE. Stage applies it as a uniform scale on a fixed 880×380 canvas. The reserved chrome geometry is subtracted from the measured region. At 1280×720 present, availH = 720−64−120 = 536, so the scale is about 1.41 and the canvas is 536px tall, which fits. At 1280×720 browse with ToC, availW = 1016 and availH = 458, so the scale is about 1.155 and the canvas is about 438px tall, which fits. At 390×844 the scale is about 0.416, which is a 158px canvas in a much larger area. The canvas stays inside its area in all four cases.

votes.rationale: Readiness comes from HTTP polling (`fetch(url)` with res.ok) of the chosen port. The only ownership check is `child.exitCode !== null`, sampled before each request. The spawn uses stdio 'ignore', so the child's own announcement is never read. Neither accepted mechanism is present: readiness is not taken from the child's announcement, and polling is not raced against the child's exit. A stale server on the port would answer the fetch before the child's exit is observed. This is possible with VERIFY_PORT, which verify.mjs passes in as a fixed port. It is also possible in the gap after findFreePort closes its probe socket. --strictPort alone is insufficient.

first_results.rationale: Unmet clause: the requirement that a persisting entity animates from its old state to its new state in place. This fails for consecutive steps that do not share a scene group. In sceneKey.ts, an ungrouped step gets its own key, `step:${step.id}`. Stage therefore mounts a new scene and cross-fades it in and out over STEP_FADE_T = 0.4s. The kit renders entities through keyed `Appear` wrappers, as SKILL.md, the template Scene and the sample Scene all show. When the incoming scene mounts fresh, every `Appear` in it starts at opacity 0 and its fade-in waits ENTER_DELAY = 0.6s, longer than the 0.4s scene fade. That wrapper encloses the layout-animated NodeBase or Arrow, so the incoming copy stays invisible while the outgoing copy fades out and while its own layout projection runs. The entity vanishes and reappears instead of morphing. The guidance names this as a fail: a fixed initial opacity of 0 with an entrance delay as long as the step transition, applied to the layout animation as well. Judges B and C cite exactly this material, and it bears them out. Judge A's pass reason is that NodeBase and Arrow set no initial opacity 0. That is true but does not decide the criterion, because the kit's documented entity path puts the hidden, delayed `Appear` around those primitives. Sync-mode AnimatePresence with absolutely positioned scenes alone does not establish a pass.

first_results.rationale: Newcomer entry path: Appear starts at opacity 0 and fades in over ENTER_T = 0.4s, after a delay that defaults to ENTER_DELAY = LAYOUT_T = 0.6s. The delay is set on Appear's own animate transition, so it applies only to the newcomer's opacity entry. Continuing-entity path: NodeBase and Arrow use `layout` and `layoutId` and set no transition prop. A persisting entity keeps its keyed Appear mounted (Scene.tsx lines 152-154), so it does not replay the delayed fade and only its layout projection runs. The sample sets no MotionConfig or layout transition anywhere; a grep for MotionConfig, transition= and LAYOUT_T finds only Stage's scene-opacity transition and test and constant uses. The continuing layout morph therefore runs on Motion's default layout transition (about 0.45s), which ends before the 0.6s newcomer delay elapses. That default comes from the Motion library, not this repo; the source establishes only that nothing overrides it. Every entity the sample introduces is rendered inside `<Appear key={id}>`. Nested identities share their parent's delayed Appear and stay invisible until it enters: the morph chips inside the link entries, reveal-label inside the reveal-frame entry, and pass-check inside a span. motion-props.test.tsx asserts that Appear's delay is at least LAYOUT_T and equals ENTER_DELAY. Judges B and C reach this verdict from the same material. Judge A's fail reason is that the continuing layout duration is not set by LAYOUT_T and not verified by a test. That does not decide the criterion. The guidance credits a fixed configured delay at least as long as the continuing layout transition, and requires no shared settlement contract or focused test. The layout path the continuing entities actually use is the unoverridden default, which is shorter than the delay.

lines.text: * Steps in the same group (same groupKey and Scene component) share a key, so the
* scene instance persists and only its payload changes. Anything else cross-fades.
style={{ position: 'absolute', left: 0, top: 0, width: '100%', height: '100%' }}
export const EASE: [number, number, number, number] = [0.22, 1, 0.36, 1]
/** Newcomers wait for persisting entities to finish their layout morph. */
* Wraps an entity that joins the scene. It fades in only after persisting entities
* have finished their layout morph, and fades out when removed from a parent
* `SceneLayer`. The fade runs once on mount: keeping the same keyed `Appear` mounted
* across steps leaves the entity untouched, so it morphs by layout projection alone.
export function Appear({ children, delay = ENTER_DELAY }: AppearProps) {
animate={{ opacity: 1, transition: { duration: ENTER_T, delay, ease: EASE } }}
exit={{ opacity: 0, transition: { duration: EXIT_T, ease: EASE } }}
style={{ position: 'absolute', left: 0, top: 0, right: 0, bottom: 0, pointerEvents: 'none' }}
- `Scene.tsx` / `steps.ts` — one `Scene` shared by all steps of a group; each step adds,
moves or removes entities. Keep a persisting entity in its keyed `Appear` so it morphs
rather than re-entering; only newcomers enter, and they enter after the others settle.

audit_results.rationale: The quoted lines show the requirement is not met. When two consecutive steps don't share a scene group, an entity present in both should animate from its old state to its new state in place. The kit's entity primitives hide the incoming copy until the outgoing copy has faded out, which is the failure the review guidance names. 1. Steps without a groupKey each get their own scene key, `step:${step.id}` (sceneKey.ts:16-20). 2. Stage puts the keyed scene inside AnimatePresence with no mode set, so the default sync mode applies. The scenes are absolutely positioned, so both stay mounted together. The outgoing scene fades out over STEP_FADE_T = 0.4s (Stage.tsx:29-42, constants.ts:9). 3. The incoming scene creates a fresh SceneLayer. Its plain `<AnimatePresence>` has no initial={false} (SceneLayer.tsx:19), so every new Appear child plays its initial state. 4. That initial state is opacity 0, and the fade-in is delayed by ENTER_DELAY = LAYOUT_T = 0.6s (Appear.tsx:17-23, constants.ts:4-7). This is longer than the 0.4s step fade. 5. Appear wraps the layout-animated NodeBase (`layout`, `layoutId={id}`, Node.tsx:27-29). The delayed opacity therefore also hides the layout morph. The morph runs for 0.6s inside an invisible parent, while the outgoing copy is gone by 0.4s. Result: the entity disappears and then fades in at its new position, instead of visibly morphing. Sync mode with out-of-flow scenes is not enough for a pass, because the guidance says the mode alone does not establish one. The delivered sample renders every entity through `<SceneLayer>` and `<Appear key={id}>` (Scene.tsx:151-154), so this is the kit's real entity path, not a hypothetical. The guidance explicitly names the ungrouped-transition scenario, so judging it here is allowed.

But the requirement is about whether the scaffold defines default presentation colors, fonts, borders, card and button styles, and theme tokens, not where they live. first_results.rationale: The verifier checks for the sample explicitly and fails with a non-zero exit that names the sample phase. After the build, verify() calls checkRegistry (scripts/verify.mjs:100-106, 174). If the reference slug is not registered in src/presentations/index.ts, it throws Failure('sample', 'presentation "…" is not registered …'). This happens before any preview or browser starts. In the render loop, a wrong step count throws Failure('sample', 'expected 9 steps, found N') (lines 130-133). For each step, compareStep checks the rendered era, title and caption against the normative OUTLINE (lines 9-51 and 77-84) and throws Failure('sample', mismatch, {step, index}) when they differ (lines 158-161). That covers outline content that is missing or out of order. main() prints `FAIL [sample]…` through formatFailure and sets process.exitCode = 1 (lines 66-69, 192-202). E2E-002 runs `npm run verify` on a copied repo (tests/e2e/helpers.ts:10-13) for two cases. In 'a missing sample (not registered)' it empties the registry array, and in 'steps out of order' it swaps two step titles. Each case asserts a non-zero status, the `FAIL [sample]` line, and no PASS (e2e-002-failures.test.ts:23-38, 95-104). Judges A and C reach this same conclusion, and the source bears it out. Judge B is right on one narrow point: if STEPS were an empty array, Header would read `step.era` from undefined (Header.tsx:21), and the run would end at the render-phase 'no [data-step-count] hook' timeout. That does not decide the criterion. The guidance credits a verifier that fails a missing sample 'at a check that reports the sample as missing or not matching the outline'. This verifier has that explicit check for an unregistered sample, a wrong step count, and wrong or reordered titles and captions, all before or independent of any later render failure. The 'only surfaces later as a render timeout' disqualifier is aimed at verifiers with no such check. Here, an empty steps array is an edge-case input the e2e plan does not name, and verification still exits non-zero for it.

audit_results.rationale: I confirm the claim from the quoted lines. The criterion requires a missing sample to make verification fail. The guidance credits a non-zero exit at an explicit check that reports the sample as missing or as not matching the outline, with output that names the build or sample phase. It counts three cases as a missing sample: the sample is not registered, its outline or steps content is absent, or that content is out of order. The quoted code covers each case. If the slug is not registered, checkRegistry throws Failure('sample', …not registered…) before the preview starts (verify.mjs:100-106, 174). If the step count is wrong, the verifier throws Failure('sample', 'expected 9 steps, found N') (130-133). If an era, title or caption is missing, wrong or out of order, compareStep checks it against the normative OUTLINE and the verifier throws Failure('sample', mismatch, {step, index}) (9-51, 77-84, 158-161). main() prints the result as 'FAIL [sample]…' and sets process.exitCode = 1 (66-69, 192-202). The end-to-end tests run the real `npm run verify` (helpers.ts:10-13) for two cases: an emptied registry and two swapped step titles. Each test asserts a non-zero status, the 'FAIL [sample]' line, and the absence of a PASS line (e2e-002-failures.test.ts:23-38, 95-104). One objection is that an empty STEPS array might crash Header and surface as a render-phase timeout. That argument depends on Header.tsx, which nobody quoted, so I don't use it to decide the claim. The quoted code also shows a count of 0 would still fail the explicit sample-phase count check. The 'render timeout only' disqualifier applies to verifiers that have no explicit sample check, and this verifier has one.

first_results.rationale: In both the repository copy and the bootstrap template copy, startPreview launches the preview server itself. It spawns process.execPath with node_modules/vite/bin/vite.js as a detached process group, with no npm or npx wrapper in between. The stop function it returns comes from installCleanup and runs killGroup(child.pid): it sends SIGTERM to the whole group (-pid), then polls isPidAlive until the process is gone. If the process is still alive when the grace period ends, it sends SIGKILL. In verify() and inspect() (both copies), chromium.launch(), page creation, the step loop and every check sit inside try, and the finally block awaits browser?.close() and then preview.stop(). So success, a failing check, a browser launch failure and any later error all pass through the cleanup, which awaits the server's exit. A readiness failure inside startPreview awaits stop() before rethrowing. SIGINT, SIGTERM and process exit are covered too. Judge C's reason is that the SIGKILL branch is not followed by another exit wait. That branch runs only if the server ignores SIGTERM for 1.5 s. The review guidance does not name that scenario, and nothing in the source shows vite preview doing it. On every exit path the guidance names, the server process is signalled directly and its exit is awaited by polling. C's point therefore does not show any clause of the requirement unmet.

first_results.rationale: The automated tests that involve a browser (E2E-001 and INT-002) never call Playwright themselves. They run `npm run verify` or `npm run inspect` with spawnSync, which returns only when the process exits. They then assert on the exit status, the output, report.json, the PNG files, the pid state and the port state. These tests contain no fixed sleeps. The only fixed setTimeout waits in the tests are in tests/unit/preview-cleanup.test.ts, where they let an `sh` process start; no browser is involved there. Judge C counts the scripts' page.waitForTimeout calls. Those calls are in the scripts, not the tests, and they do not replace a state wait. In verify.mjs, waitForTimeout(SETTLE_MS) runs only after the step-index waitForFunction succeeds (or, for the first step, after waitForSelector on '[data-step-count]'). In inspect, the step-index waitForFunction comes first. waitForSettle's fixed delay is then followed by a polling waitForFunction on document.getAnimations(). Every state check is therefore a polling or auto-waiting wait. The extra fixed settle is a 'longer fixed settle delay', which the guidance classes as validator noise. C's reason does not decide the requirement.

results.rationale: I rule with judges A and B. In all four script copies (repository and bootstrap verify and inspect), startPreview spawns `process.execPath` running node_modules/vite/bin/vite.js directly, with `detached: true` (preview.mjs:95-112). No npm or npx wrapper sits in between, so the child pid is the server process and leads its own process group. Its stop function is `installCleanup(() => killGroup(child.pid), ...)` (line 104). killGroup sends SIGTERM to `-pid`, the whole group, then polls `isPidAlive` every 50 ms during the grace period (lines 29-41). isPidAlive (lines 19-26) is `process.kill(pid, 0)`, which returns false once the process no longer exists. If readiness fails, startPreview awaits stop() before rethrowing (lines 105-110). verify() runs chromium.launch(), newPage and renderSteps inside `try`, and the `finally` awaits `browser?.close()` and then `preview.stop()` (verify.mjs:180-189, same in the bootstrap copy). So success, a failing check, a browser launch failure and any later error all pass through that cleanup. In inspect(), `outputDir(...)` (line 196) sits between startPreview and `try`, which the auditor raised. It cannot throw on any path the script takes. The script's only entry point, main(), calls inspect with `parseArgs(...)` (lines 235-243). parseArgs rejects any slug that fails `SLUG = /^[a-z0-9]+(-[a-z0-9]+)*$/` before inspect runs (line 32). For a slug that passes, `path.join(artifacts, slug)` is always a direct child of OUT_DIR, so none of outputDir's throw conditions can hold (lines 42-50). Everything after it is inside try/finally with `await preview.stop()` (lines 198-232). The bootstrap copies are identical (parity.test.ts asserts byte equality). Signals and a bare process exit are also covered by installCleanup. Judge C's reason is that after the grace period killGroup sends SIGKILL without polling again. That branch runs only when a server ignores SIGTERM for 1.5 s, and nothing cited shows vite preview doing so. SIGKILL to the group cannot be ignored, and the focused test 'escalates to SIGKILL when SIGTERM is ignored' confirms the group dies. The E2E tests confirm that after both passing and failing verify runs the preview pid is no longer running and its port is closed. A hypothetical that the source does not produce does not make the requirement unmet.

results.rationale: I rule with judges A and B. The test suites are defined by three configs. vitest.config.ts runs src/**/*.test.* in jsdom and tests/unit in node, so no browser is involved. vitest.e2e.config.ts runs tests/e2e. vitest.integration.config.ts runs tests/integration, which its own comment calls the browser-backed tests. The browser-backed tests are E2E-001, E2E-002, INT-001 and INT-002. Each drives a browser only by running `npm run verify` or `npm run inspect` through the synchronous spawnSync helpers: e2e helpers.ts `verify` (lines 10-13) and integration run.ts `run` (lines 1-18). Each spawnSync call returns only after that run has finished and exited. The tests then assert on its exit status, its output, the report and screenshot files it wrote, and the pid and port state. None of these tests calls setTimeout, waitForTimeout or any other sleep, and none reads a count right after an action as if it had waited. INT-002 lines 1-107 contain only fixture source text, the `run` import and a beforeAll that runs build and inspect synchronously. Judge C's reason is that the scripts these tests run call page.waitForTimeout (verify's SETTLE_MS of 800, and inspect's settleMs). This criterion judges the tests' own waits. The scripts never use a fixed sleep in place of a state wait. Each ArrowRight is followed by `page.waitForFunction` polling until `data-step-index` equals the target index (verify.mjs:137-154, inspect:209-212). Inspect also polls `document.getAnimations()` until finite animations finish and refuses to capture an unsettled step (lines 177-187). The extra fixed settle delays come after those state waits, and guidance lists longer fixed settle delays as validator noise. So Judge C's reason does not show that a browser test sleeps instead of waiting for state. The only fixed `setTimeout(r, 200)` waits in tests are in tests/unit/preview-cleanup.test.ts, which spawns `sh` processes and does not drive a browser.

result.rationale: I rule with judges A and B. In all four script copies (repository and bootstrap verify and inspect), startPreview spawns `process.execPath` running node_modules/vite/bin/vite.js directly, with `detached: true` (preview.mjs:95-112). No npm or npx wrapper sits in between, so the child pid is the server process and leads its own process group. Its stop function is `installCleanup(() => killGroup(child.pid), ...)` (line 104). killGroup sends SIGTERM to `-pid`, the whole group, then polls `isPidAlive` every 50 ms during the grace period (lines 29-41). isPidAlive (lines 19-26) is `process.kill(pid, 0)`, which returns false once the process no longer exists. If readiness fails, startPreview awaits stop() before rethrowing (lines 105-110). verify() runs chromium.launch(), newPage and renderSteps inside `try`, and the `finally` awaits `browser?.close()` and then `preview.stop()` (verify.mjs:180-189, same in the bootstrap copy). So success, a failing check, a browser launch failure and any later error all pass through that cleanup. In inspect(), `outputDir(...)` (line 196) sits between startPreview and `try`, which the auditor raised. It cannot throw on any path the script takes. The script's only entry point, main(), calls inspect with `parseArgs(...)` (lines 235-243). parseArgs rejects any slug that fails `SLUG = /^[a-z0-9]+(-[a-z0-9]+)*$/` before inspect runs (line 32). For a slug that passes, `path.join(artifacts, slug)` is always a direct child of OUT_DIR, so none of outputDir's throw conditions can hold (lines 42-50). Everything after it is inside try/finally with `await preview.stop()` (lines 198-232). The bootstrap copies are identical (parity.test.ts asserts byte equality). Signals and a bare process exit are also covered by installCleanup. Judge C's reason is that after the grace period killGroup sends SIGKILL without polling again. That branch runs only when a server ignores SIGTERM for 1.5 s, and nothing cited shows vite preview doing so. SIGKILL to the group cannot be ignored, and the focused test 'escalates to SIGKILL when SIGTERM is ignored' confirms the group dies. The E2E tests confirm that after both passing and failing verify runs the preview pid is no longer running and its port is closed. A hypothetical that the source does not produce does not make the requirement unmet.

presentation-skill.rationale: The auditor's facts are accurate, but they don't defeat this criterion's pass. The review guidance for skill-empty-directory-scaffold lists what to require: (1) the bootstrap template has the build setup, scene kit and presentation index with the required dependency set; (2) SKILL.md directs a full scaffold with dependency installation for an empty target; (3) a test materializes the template in a fresh temporary location and builds it; (4) the scene-kit snapshot matches the canonical kit; (5) Chromium is installed or checked for. Style neutrality is not on that list. The rubric gives it its own criterion, skill-scaffold-style-neutral, which says to inspect the bootstrap template's dependencies and styles. The core scenario only asks for a full scaffold of the three anchors plus dependency installation before the presentation is created, and the material shows that happening. Separately, the styles the auditor cites sit in a presentation-owned file, src/presentations/example/talk.css. Its own header says the scene kit ships no styles. That file is applied only through the example Talk's className. The kit itself adds no styling framework and no CSS, so this styling is not clearly a scaffold styling default. Either way, the stated reason is a style-neutrality question that this criterion's guidance assigns elsewhere, so it cannot turn this pass into a fail.
